title: Fear of death
hook: meeting fear of death with breath and kindness
tomorrow: if life is this short, what's the first thing to do with it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, your wishes: writing down how you'd like to be cared for at the end. Thinking ahead. Writing it can stir up something older and quieter. Today, that feeling itself.

Search bars hear what people won't say out loud. Late at night someone types: is it normal to be scared of dying? Long before search bars, a brahmin named Janussoni walked up to the Buddha with his answer already settled. Everyone who has to die, he said, is afraid of death, terrified of it. No exceptions. It isn't a cruel claim. It sounds like plain honesty. And the Buddha doesn't nod along.
screen: `IS IT NORMAL TO BE SCARED OF DYING?` → `EVERYONE IS, SAYS JANUSSONI.` → `THE BUDDHA DOESN'T NOD ALONG.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya, and the Buddha's answer is a sorting, not a scolding. Some people fear death and some don't, he says. Here is who fears. One is still hungry for sense pleasures; when a serious illness comes, the thought arrives: the pleasures I love will be taken from me. He grieves and weeps and beats his breast. Another clings to the body itself: this body I love will be taken. A third has done harm and left good undone, and dreads where that leads. A fourth is in doubt about the teaching, with nothing firm to stand on. Then the Buddha turns each one over. The one who has let go of craving, who isn't clinging to the body, who has done good and harmed no one, who has no doubt about the teaching: when illness comes, that person isn't terrified. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't call fear a failure, or say a good follower feels none. He treats fear of death the way a doctor treats a fever: something with causes you can find. That's the part worth telling a friend tonight. The old answer here isn't be braver. It's look closer. A root you can name is a root you can work with, slowly, across a life. Janussoni hears it and asks to be counted among the Buddha's followers.
screen: `NOT EVERYONE FEARS DEATH.` · `FOUR ROOTS: WANTING, BODY, REGRET, DOUBT.` · `A FEVER WITH CAUSES.` · `LOOK CLOSER, NOT BRAVER.` · then, large: `MEET THE FEAR.`

segments.voice: Let one fear about death come forward, small enough to hold. Breathe in and ask which root it grows from: wanting, the body, regret or doubt. Breathe out, and stay beside it kindly, the way you'd sit with a scared kid, without pushing it away.
Fear of death: the dread of dying. In this sutta it has four roots, wanting, the body, regret and doubt, and each one can be seen.
Your line: meet the fear. Fear has roots, and roots can be seen. Two days left in this block.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers who lead reflection on death sometimes pair it with recalling one's own good deeds and trust in the teaching, the same roots this sutta names; some temples offer this in classes on death and dying.

fork.setup: a friend's dad has a health scare. he says he isn't scared of dying; he's scared he never made peace with his brother. which root is that?
options: regret: good left undone, still waiting to be done.
the body: he's clinging to his health and strength.
doubt: he isn't sure what he believes about death.
fork.reveal: that's the third root: harm done or good left undone. it's also the one root that can still be worked on while he's alive.

original.note: Pali: fear, dread. The sutta's name, Abhaya, adds a- (not): fearless.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm, wise person feels no fear of death.
what it means: the Buddha sorts people who fear death from those who don't, and names what feeds the fear: craving, clinging to the body, regret, doubt.
what a scholar hears: AN 4.184, the Abhaya (fearless) Sutta, answers the brahmin Janussoni's claim point by point, four who fear and four who don't.

chat.meaning: The Buddha didn't scold fear or call it unavoidable. He named its roots so a person could look at them and work with them.

tie.story: Janussoni said everyone fears death; the Buddha named what the fear grows from: wanting, the body, regret, doubt.
tie.friend: Mai can look at her 2am fear for Ông, and for herself, one root at a time instead of running from it.
tie.you: what's one fear you could sit beside kindly this week?

Janussoni.meaning: a brahmin who told the Buddha everyone fears death

brahmin.meaning: a member of ancient India's priestly class

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's talks arranged by number

sutta.meaning: a discourse of the Buddha, in Pali

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.184 (Abhaya Sutta: Janussoni claims everyone fears death; the Buddha names four who fear and four who don't)

notes: AN 4.184 paraphrased throughout: the four who fear (not free of lust for sense pleasures; not free of lust for the body; has done no good and has done harm; has doubt about the true Dhamma) and the four who don't; the grieving, lamenting and beating the breast; Janussoni going for refuge at the end.
